title: Surface roughness of turned parts
intro:
Twenty-four steel shafts were turned at different feeds (mm per revolution) and cutting speeds (m/min), and the surface roughness Ra (µm) of each was measured. The model is Ra = b₀ + b₁·Feed + b₂·Speed. How well would it predict the roughness of new parts?

Find the **in-sample RMSE**, the **leave-one-out cross-validated RMSE** (k = n = 24), and the **hold-out test RMSE** with a quarter of the rows held out and the program's seed 4. Give each to three decimals or more. The hold-out rows come from the program's own seeded shuffle, so use the Workbench for that one; the other two you can also get in Python or R.

To use the Workbench: press **Copy the data**, press Ctrl+B, click **+ Data table** and paste (Ctrl+V). Choose **Multiple regression** and set **Data table** to the table you pasted, **Response column (y)** to *Ra*, **Predictor columns** to *Feed, Speed*, **Variable selection** to *All the predictors listed*, **Cross-validation folds (k)** to 24, **Hold-out share** to 0.25 and **Hold-out seed** to 4. The three RMSEs are near the end of the results. Ctrl+L brings you back.

ask.wrong: Check that Hold-out share is 0.25 and Hold-out seed is 4, and that both predictors are listed.

InSampleRmse.says: That is the residual standard error σ̂, which divides SS error by n − p = 21. The in-sample RMSE divides by n = 24: √(SS error/n).

CvRmse.says: That is 5-fold cross-validation, the Workbench's default. Leave-one-out uses k = n: set Cross-validation folds (k) to 24.

HoldOutRmse.says: That matches the in-sample RMSE, on rows the model was fitted to (and, by chance, the hold-out RMSE for seed 1, the Workbench's default). The hold-out RMSE uses only the six test rows drawn by seed 4, with the model fitted to the other eighteen.

hints: In-sample RMSE = √(SS error/n): fit the model to all 24 rows and take the root of the mean squared residual.

Leave-one-out: leave out each row in turn, fit to the other 23, predict the one left out; RMSE = √(Σ(yᵢ − ŷ₍ᵢ₎)²/24). For least squares there is a shortcut: ŷ₍ᵢ₎'s error is eᵢ/(1 − hᵢᵢ), so in R sqrt(mean((residuals(fit) / (1 - hatvalues(fit)))^2)).
The hold-out RMSE depends on which rows are drawn. 0.25 × 24 = 6 rows; the Workbench lists them under Rows in the test set. Its Code tab writes the same calculation in Python and R with those rows.
